summary: This RFC describes the RPL Option, an IPv6 hop-by-hop option for RPL routers to carry routing information in data packets. This helps quickly spot inconsistencies in the routing topology.

eli5.summary: Each message carries a tiny note about its route, so helper nodes can notice quickly if something is going wrong.

questions: how does rpl detect routing loops
subtitle: An IPv6 hop-by-hop option that lets RPL routers stamp routing information onto data packets to catch loops and inconsistencies fast.

tldr.problem: RPL networks are low-power and lossy, so control traffic must be kept small, yet routing inconsistencies such as loops still need to be found and fixed quickly.
tldr.mechanism: Routers carry a small RPL Option (type 0x63) in an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop header on data packets. It holds flags, an RPL instance ID and the sender's rank, and each RPL router processes and updates it.
tldr.outcome: Inconsistencies are detected on the data path itself, so repair traffic is only generated when there is data traffic. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that has since been updated by later RFCs.

today: RFC 6553 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2012. It has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 9008, RFC 9685 and RFC 9914, so read those with it.

sections.title: Why Check Routes in the Data
sections.content:
RPL is a distance vector IPv6 routing protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs), which are typically constrained in energy and channel capacity. A routing protocol there must generate control traffic sparingly. That is at odds with the need to spread new routing information quickly when something is wrong.

RPL resolves this by using a slow proactive process to build and maintain the topology, with low-rate beaconing in the steady state, and a reactive process for inconsistencies. When it detects one, it temporarily raises the beacon rate. The beacon rate is governed by dynamic Trickle timers from RFC 6206.

Unlike OSPF (RFC 2328), RPL finds inconsistencies by data-path verification: the routing information rides inside the datagram itself. The motivation is that control traffic should be bounded by the data traffic. If nobody is sending data, there is no need to fix routing problems that may be temporary.
sections.eli5: Sending lots of "are we lost?" messages would waste the tiny batteries. So instead, the messages people are already sending carry a little route note, and problems only get fixed when someone is actually sending something.

sections.title: Overview of the RPL Option
sections.content:
RPL builds a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) that tries to minimise path cost to the DAG root. Loops can still occur in some circumstances, and RPL is designed to use a data-path loop detection method. Loop detection is one known requirement, and the RFC notes that other data-path uses might be defined in the future.

The RPL Option is a new IPv6 option carried in the Hop-by-Hop header. It is only for use between RPL routers in the same RPL Instance. Every RPL router along a packet's delivery path processes and updates it. If a received packet has no RPL Option, the router must insert one before forwarding to another RPL router.

The RFC also specifies IPv6-in-IPv6 tunneling (RFC 2473) when attaching the option. Tunneling keeps the original packet unmodified and makes ICMP errors return to the source of the RPL Option rather than to the source of the original packet.
sections.eli5: Every helper along the way reads the note on the message, updates it and passes it on. If a message has no note, the helper wraps it in an extra envelope that has one.

sections.title: The RPL Option Format
sections.content:
The option sits in an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop Options header immediately after the IPv6 header, with an alignment requirement of 2n. The Option Type is 0x63. Opt Data Len is an 8-bit length in octets, excluding the Option Type and Opt Data Len fields, and it is variable.

The fixed fields are three 1-bit flags, five zero bits, an 8-bit RPLInstanceID and a 16-bit SenderRank. They are O (Down), R (Rank-Error) and F (Forwarding-Error). All are defined in Section 11.2 of RFC 6550, and processing follows the rules there. Optional sub-TLVs may follow, but none are defined in this document.

The two high-order bits of the Option Type are 01 and the third bit is 1. According to RFC 2460, a node that does not understand the option MUST discard the packet, and the values are expected to change en route. A RPL device MUST skip any unrecognized sub-TLVs and try to process any that follow.
sections.eli5: The note has a few on/off switches, a number saying which road map it belongs to, and a number saying how far the sender is from the destination. A helper who cannot read this kind of note must throw the message away.

sections.title: How RPL Routers Handle the Option
sections.content:
Datagrams sent between RPL routers MUST include a RPL Option or a RPL Source Route Header (RFC 6554), and MAY include both. A datagram with a source routing header does not need the option, since the source and intermediate routers ensure that header has no loops.

If the router is the source of the original packet and the destination is known to be in the same RPL Instance, it SHOULD put the option directly in the original packet. Otherwise it MUST use IPv6-in-IPv6 tunneling and place the option in the tunnel header. The router picks the next RPL router to process the packet as the tunnel exit-point. That may be the last RPL router on the path, or, for example, a DODAG parent, in which case the packet may cross several tunnels.

A router that receives a tunnel packet addressed to it MUST process the RPL Option before decapsulation. If it then forwards the original packet to another RPL router, it MUST encapsulate again with the option. Fields that do not change hop-by-hop MUST stay the same as received.

Routers must keep the option inside the RPL network: packets for the router itself are handled normally (removing the outer header also removes the option), packets for elsewhere in the same instance are forwarded, and packets for nodes outside the instance are dropped if the outermost header carries a RPL Option the forwarding router did not generate.

Tunneling adds headers. To avoid fragmentation the RFC says it is desirable to have an MTU of at least 1280 + 40 (outer IP header) + RPL_OPTION_MAX_SIZE. Some links, such as 6LoWPAN links at 1280 octets, cannot offer that, but most traffic is expected to be much smaller than the MTU.
sections.eli5: If you are sending to a friend on the same team, you can write the note straight on the message. Otherwise you put the message in a bigger envelope and write the note on the envelope. The envelope comes off at the other end, so the note never leaves the team.

sections.title: Attacks Using the Option
sections.content:
The RPL Option helps routers detect routing inconsistencies. The message security mechanisms of RFC 6550 do not apply to it.

DAG inconsistency: by abusing the Down O flag and SenderRank, an attacker can make routers believe the RPL Instance is inconsistent. That makes a router reset its DIO Trickle timer and send DIO messages more often. An implementation MAY limit these resets to MAX_RPL_OPTION_RANK_ERRORS per hour, with a RECOMMENDED value of 20.

DAO inconsistency: in Storing mode, routers keep Downward routing state, and the Forwarding-Error F flag tells a router that a child could not deliver a datagram. An attacker can use it to make a router discard Downward state. An implementation MAY limit this to MAX_RPL_OPTION_FORWARD_ERRORS per hour, again RECOMMENDED at 20. In Non-Storing mode only the LBR keeps Downward state, so the option cannot be used for this attack.
sections.eli5: A trickster could write false notes to make helpers panic and shout much more than they should. So helpers are allowed to ignore the panic after a set number of alarms per hour.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned hex value 0x63 (binary act 01, chg 1, rest 00011) to the RPL Option in the Destination Options and Hop-by-Hop Options registry. The first two bits tell an IPv6 node to discard the packet if it does not recognize the option, and the third bit says the data may change en route.

IANA also created a registry called RPL-option-TLV for the sub-TLVs carried in the option. New codes may be allocated only by IETF Review (RFC 5226), and the type is an 8-bit field with values from 0 to 255.
sections.eli5: The RFC asks the official list-keepers to reserve one special code number for this note, and to start a list for any extra labels people add later.

fields.name: Opt Data Len
fields.desc: Length of the option in octets, excluding Option Type and Opt Data Len.

fields.name: O
fields.desc: Down flag, as defined in Section 11.2 of RFC 6550.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Rank-Error flag, as defined in Section 11.2 of RFC 6550.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Forwarding-Error flag, as defined in Section 11.2 of RFC 6550.

fields.name: RPLInstanceID
fields.desc: Identifies the RPL Instance, as defined in Section 11.2 of RFC 6550.

fields.name: SenderRank
fields.desc: Rank of the sender, as defined in Section 11.2 of RFC 6550.
